title: Instructions, Rules and Advice
overview: Unit 11 gave you have to, which says something is necessary. This unit gives you the form that closes a door instead of opening one, and it is deliberately taught apart from the other so the two never blur. It also covers the compressed English of public signs — where whole clauses vanish and the meaning has to be reconstructed. It ends with a real safety notice, because a sign you misread is worse than one you cannot read at all.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 exists to be kept apart from Unit 11 — read the comparison twice.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a safety notice and a set of signs.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the one that separates the two negatives.
Record yourself explaining three rules and reading four signs.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
This unit finishes something Unit 11 started, and the two halves were separated on purpose.
In Unit 11 you learned have to, which means something is necessary, and do not have to, which means it is not necessary. Every negative in that unit opened a door. Nothing was forbidden.
This unit teaches the form that forbids.
Must. It means something is necessary — the same as have to, near enough.
You must wear safety shoes. All staff must sign in.
And must not, contracted to mustn't. This is the important one. It means something is forbidden.
You must not enter this area. You mustn't touch that.
So now compare the two negatives, and this is the whole reason for two separate units.
You do not have to wear a uniform. No uniform is required. Wear one if you want.
You must not wear a uniform. Uniforms are forbidden.
Those are opposite meanings and they are one small word apart. If you learn them in the same lesson they blur. Learning them six units apart, each with its own examples, keeps them separate — and the test is simple: do not have to opens, must not closes.
A few practical things about must.
It takes the plain verb, and it never changes. I must, she must, they must. No -s.
It makes its own questions and negatives, with no do — must I go, you mustn't. Like can from Unit 3, not like have to from Unit 11.
And in real speech, must is less common than you would expect for obligation. People say have to more often. Where must dominates is written rules — signs, contracts, safety notices, official instructions. So you will read must far more often than you will say it, and mustn't is the one you actually need to recognise instantly.
Second pattern: the other ways English says allowed and not allowed.
Can, which you have had since Unit 3, does permission as well as ability. You can park here. You can't park here.
And on signs, English uses a compressed form: no plus a verb with -ing.
No smoking. No parking. No entry. No eating or drinking.
That is a complete prohibition in two words. There is no verb, no subject and no modal, and it is one of the most compressed structures in English.
There is also allowed and not allowed, which is what people actually say when explaining a rule to somebody. Smoking is not allowed in here. You're not allowed to park there. It is softer than must not and it is what you will hear from a colleague rather than read on a wall.
So you now have three registers for the same idea. No smoking is the sign. Smoking is not allowed is the explanation. You mustn't smoke here is the instruction. Same rule, three levels of directness, and knowing which is which tells you a lot about who is speaking.
Third pattern: reading a public sign.
Signs delete words. That is their whole design, and it means the reader has to put the missing words back.
Mind the step. Missing: you should. Danger: deep water. Missing: there is, and stay away. Authorised personnel only. Missing: may enter this area.
The skill is reconstruction, and there are three questions that do it.
Who is this addressed to? Everybody, or only some people? Staff only and authorised personnel only look similar and mean different things.
Is it an instruction or information? Mind the step tells you to do something. Deep water tells you a fact and leaves the conclusion to you.
And what happens if you ignore it? A sign about a fine is a rule. A sign about deep water is a warning. Those are enforced differently and read differently.
One last thing worth knowing. On signs, the most important word is often the last one, because the qualifying phrase comes at the end. No parking is absolute. No parking between 8am and 6pm is not. If you stop reading at the second word, you have read the wrong sign — and that is by far the most common mistake with English signage.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: Something you must or must not do in a particular place.
words.example: It is a rule, not a suggestion.
practice: There is one rule everybody forgets.
words.starter: It is a rule, not a
words.tutor: Say one rule where you work or live. Use must.

words.meaning: A board with words or a picture giving information or an instruction.
words.example: There is a sign on the door.
words.starter: There is a sign on the
words.tutor: Say what a sign near you says, in full sentences rather than sign English.

words.meaning: Something that tells you about a possible danger.
words.example: That is a warning, not a rule.
practice: The warning is on the label.
It is a warning about deep water.
words.starter: That is a warning, not a
words.tutor: Say the difference between a warning and a rule in your own words.

words.meaning: The possibility of harm.
words.example: Danger: deep water.
practice: It is a danger to everybody.
words.tutor: Danger on a sign means stay away. Say the full sentence it stands for.

words.meaning: The state of being protected from harm.
words.example: You must wear safety shoes.
practice: The safety equipment is by the door.
words.tutor: Say safety shoes, safety notice, safety rule. It goes in front of a noun.

words.meaning: Not in danger; not causing harm.
words.example: It is safe now.
practice: Is it safe to go in?
It is not safe to lift that alone.
Keep it in a safe place.
words.tutor: Say safe and safety in two sentences. One is an adjective, one is a noun.

words.meaning: To let somebody do something.
words.example: Smoking is not allowed in here.
practice: You are not allowed to park there.
They do not allow bags in the room.
Are we allowed to use this?
words.tutor: Not allowed is softer than must not. Say the same rule both ways.

words.meaning: Being told you may do something.
words.example: You need permission to enter.
words.tutor: Say ask permission and have permission. Both are common.

words.meaning: Not allowed at all.
words.example: It is forbidden to smoke here.
practice: It is not forbidden — it is just not usual.
words.tutor: Forbidden is very strong and quite formal. Say where you would actually see it.

words.meaning: The act of going in, or the way in.
words.example: The sign says no entry.
practice: Entry is by the side door.
words.tutor: No entry is two words standing for a whole sentence. Say the full sentence.

words.meaning: The way out.
words.example: Keep the exit clear at all times.
practice: The exit is at the back.
Use the fire exit only in an emergency.
words.starter: Keep the exit clear at all
words.tutor: Ask where the nearest exit is. It is worth knowing before you need it.

words.meaning: Limited to certain people or certain times.
words.example: This is a restricted area.
practice: It is a restricted route for vehicles.
The area is restricted to staff.
words.tutor: Restricted means limited, not banned. Say the difference from forbidden.

words.meaning: The tools and machines used for a job.
words.example: Check the equipment before you start.
practice: You must not use the equipment without training.
The safety equipment is by the door.
words.tutor: Equipment has no plural. Say a piece of equipment, not an equipment.

words.meaning: To keep something or somebody safe from harm.
words.example: Safety shoes protect your feet.
practice: This is to protect everybody, not just you.
words.tutor: Say protect against something. That is the usual pattern.

words.meaning: The chance that something bad will happen.
words.example: There is a risk of falling.
practice: It is not worth the risk.
The risk is small but it is real.
words.tutor: Say at your own risk. It means nobody else is responsible if it goes wrong.

words.meaning: To keep away from, or to stop something happening.
words.example: Avoid parking under trees.
words.tutor: Notice avoid takes -ing: avoid parking, avoid lifting. Say both.

words.meaning: Something that could cause harm.
words.example: A wet floor is a hazard.
practice: The main hazard here is the traffic.
There are two hazards on this list.
words.tutor: Hazard is the thing; risk is the chance. Say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: A loud sound warning of danger.
words.example: If the alarm sounds, leave immediately.
practice: The alarm is tested every Monday.
The fire alarm went off at two.
words.tutor: Say what you do if the alarm sounds. Use the imperative from Unit 6.

groups.title: What the notice tells you to do

words.meaning: To have clothing or equipment on your body.
words.example: You must wear safety shoes in this area.
practice: You do not have to wear a uniform.
She was wearing a blue jacket.
You must not wear loose clothing near the machines.
words.starter: You must wear safety shoes in this
words.tutor: Say you must wear and you do not have to wear. Notice how different they are.

words.meaning: To take something away or take it off.
words.example: Remove the label before use.
practice: Remove your equipment at the end of the shift.
The sign was removed last week.
You must remove all bags from the aisle.
words.tutor: Remove is more formal than take off. Say where you would see each.

words.meaning: To push something down, usually a button.
words.example: Press the green button to start.
practice: Press and hold for three seconds.
words.tutor: Say press, push and pull in three instructions. They are not the same.

words.meaning: To move something away from you.
words.example: Push the door — do not pull it.
practice: Push the trolley, do not carry it.
words.tutor: Push and pull are opposites and both appear on doors. Say both.

words.meaning: To move something towards you.
words.example: Pull the handle down.
words.tutor: Say pull the handle. Then say the opposite instruction.

words.meaning: To turn something on or off.
words.example: Switch off the machine before cleaning it.
practice: Switch it on at the wall.
The switch is on the left.
Switch off at the end of the shift.
words.starter: Switch off the machine before cleaning
words.tutor: Say switch on and switch off. Both take a small word after switch.

words.meaning: Burning that causes damage and danger.
words.example: In case of fire, use the stairs.
practice: The fire alarm is tested on Mondays.
There was a small fire last year.
Do not use the lift in a fire.
The fire exit is at the back.
words.starter: In case of fire, use the
words.tutor: Say in case of fire. It is the standard opening on this kind of notice.

words.meaning: The act or route of getting away from danger.
words.example: Keep the escape route clear.
practice: There is no other escape route.
Do not block the escape route.
The escape route is marked in green.
words.tutor: Say escape route. Then say where the nearest one is from where you are.

words.meaning: To leave a building because of danger.
words.example: Evacuate the building immediately.
practice: We had to evacuate twice last year.
The building was evacuated at ten.
words.tutor: Evacuate is formal and appears almost only on notices. Say the everyday version too.

words.meaning: To gather together in one place.
words.example: Assemble in the car park.
practice: The assembly point is by the gate.
Assemble and wait to be counted.
Do not assemble near the building.
words.tutor: Say where the assembly point is where you work or study. If you do not know, that is worth finding out.

words.meaning: A container of material for putting out a fire.
words.example: The extinguisher is beside the door.
practice: You must not use an extinguisher without training.
There are two extinguishers on this floor.
The extinguisher was checked in March.
words.tutor: Say the word slowly: ex-tin-guish-er. Four syllables.

readings.title: One Word Apart, Opposite Meanings
readings.passage:
There is a pair in English that means opposite things and differs by one small word. It is worth ten minutes of your attention.
You do not have to wear a uniform.
You must not wear a uniform.
The first says no uniform is required — wear one if you like, nobody minds. The second says uniforms are forbidden.
Unit 11 taught the first. This unit teaches the second, and the six-unit gap between them is deliberate. Learners who meet both in the same lesson tend to blur them permanently, because the two forms look similar, sound similar and sit in the same grammatical slot. Meeting them far apart, each with its own examples and its own reading, keeps them separate.
The test is short enough to keep in your head. Do not have to opens a door. Must not closes one.
Why does this matter beyond an exercise? Because both appear constantly in the places where getting it wrong is expensive — job advertisements, contracts, safety notices, tenancy agreements. You do not have to have experience is an invitation. You must not operate this without training is a prohibition with consequences.
And there is an asymmetry worth noticing. Misreading do not have to as a prohibition costs you an opportunity you never knew you had — a job you did not apply for. Misreading must not as merely optional costs you something more immediate. Neither error is small, and they fail in opposite directions.

readings.title: How to Read a Sign
readings.passage:
Signs delete words. That is their design, and it means reading one is an act of reconstruction rather than translation.
Mind the step stands for you should mind the step. Danger: deep water stands for there is deep water here and you should stay away from it. Authorised personnel only stands for only authorised personnel may enter this area.
Three questions put the missing words back.
Who is this addressed to? Everybody, or only some people? Staff only and authorised personnel only look similar and are not the same — the first names a group you might belong to, the second names a permission you have to have been given.
Is it an instruction or information? Mind the step tells you to do something. Deep water tells you a fact and leaves the conclusion to you. Both change your behaviour; only one tells you how.
What happens if you ignore it? A sign mentioning a fine is a rule enforced by somebody. A sign mentioning deep water is a warning enforced by physics. They are read differently and they should be.
And then the mistake almost everybody makes, including people reading in their first language.
The most important word on a sign is often the last one, because the qualifying phrase comes at the end.
No parking is absolute.
No parking between 8am and 6pm is not.
No parking except for loading is not.
If you stop reading at the second word you have read a different sign from the one in front of you, and you will be confident about it. Read every sign to the end, particularly the short ones, because the short ones are the ones you think you have already understood.

readings.title: The Notice, and Four Signs
readings.setting: A safety notice inside a workplace, and four signs on doors along the same corridor.
readings.passage:
SAFETY NOTICE - LOADING BAY
  Northfield Warehouse

  YOU MUST
    · wear safety shoes at all times
    · report any damaged equipment
    · keep the escape route clear

  YOU MUST NOT
    · operate the lifting equipment
      without training
    · stack above the marked line
    · use an extinguisher you have not
      been trained on

  YOU DO NOT HAVE TO
    · wear a helmet in this bay
      (helmets are required in Bay 3)

  IN CASE OF FIRE
    Sound the alarm. Evacuate by the
    nearest exit. Assemble in the staff
    car park. Do not use the lift.

  Reviewed 4 January. Next review January.

-----------------------------------------

  FOUR SIGNS ON THE SAME CORRIDOR

   [1]  NO ENTRY

   [2]  NO PARKING
        except for loading

   [3]  AUTHORISED PERSONNEL ONLY

   [4]  DANGER
        Deep excavation
        Keep to the marked path

comprehension.q: What is the difference between you do not have to wear a uniform and you must not wear a uniform?
comprehension.a: The first means no uniform is required — wear one if you like. The second means uniforms are forbidden.
comprehension.why: Opposite meanings, one small word apart. This is the pair the whole unit is built around.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say the two forms are taught six units apart?
comprehension.a: Because learners who meet both in the same lesson tend to blur them permanently — they look similar, sound similar and sit in the same grammatical slot.
comprehension.why: The separation is a teaching decision with a reason, and knowing the reason helps a learner keep them apart deliberately.

comprehension.q: What asymmetry does the text describe between the two errors?
comprehension.a: Misreading do not have to as a prohibition costs you an opportunity you never knew you had. Misreading must not as optional costs you something more immediate.
comprehension.why: The two failures are not the same size or the same kind, and naming that makes both worth avoiding for different reasons.

comprehension.q: What does authorised personnel only stand for in full?
comprehension.a: Only authorised personnel may enter this area.
comprehension.why: Reconstruction is the whole skill. The sign has deleted a verb, a modal and an object, and all three have to be put back.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between staff only and authorised personnel only?
comprehension.a: Staff only names a group you might belong to. Authorised personnel only names a permission you have to have been given.
comprehension.why: They look almost identical and one is much narrower. Being staff does not make you authorised.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say the last word on a sign is often the most important?
comprehension.a: Because the qualifying phrase comes at the end — no parking is absolute, but no parking except for loading is not.
comprehension.why: Stopping early produces a confident misreading, which is worse than not reading at all. The short signs are the riskiest for exactly this reason.

comprehension.q: The notice says you do not have to wear a helmet in this bay. What does that mean, and what does the bracket add?
comprehension.a: It means a helmet is not required in this bay — you may wear one if you want. The bracket adds that helmets are required in Bay 3, so the rule changes by location.
comprehension.why: This is the one open door on the notice, and it sits directly under six closed ones, which is exactly where the confusion would occur if the two forms had not been separated.

comprehension.q: You have been trained on lifting equipment but not on extinguishers. What may you do and not do?
comprehension.a: You may operate the lifting equipment, because the prohibition applies only without training. You must not use an extinguisher, because you have not been trained on one.
comprehension.why: Both prohibitions are conditional on training and the conditions are separate. Reading either one as absolute gets the answer wrong in a different direction.

comprehension.q: Sign 2 says NO PARKING except for loading. What would you have misread if you stopped at the second word?
comprehension.a: You would have read an absolute prohibition, when in fact parking for loading is permitted.
comprehension.why: This is the mistake Reading 2 predicts, printed on a sign so it can be caught. The qualifier is on the second line and easy to skip.

comprehension.q: The fire instructions tell you to assemble in the staff car park. What do they not tell you?
comprehension.a: They do not say what to do if the staff car park cannot be reached, or who checks that everybody is out.
comprehension.why: The instructions are complete for the ordinary case and silent on the case where the ordinary route is blocked, which is the situation they exist for.

grammar.title: Must and mustn't
grammar.explanation: Must says something is necessary. Mustn't says something is forbidden. This card exists to be kept apart from Unit 11's do not have to, which means the opposite of mustn't.
grammar.rule:
MUST — it is necessary
  You must wear safety shoes.
  All staff must sign in.

MUSTN'T — it is FORBIDDEN
  You must not enter this area.
  You mustn't touch that.

THE PAIR THAT MATTERS — one word apart:
  You DON'T HAVE TO wear a uniform.
     -> not required. Wear one if you like.
  You MUSTN'T wear a uniform.
     -> forbidden.

  don't have to  OPENS a door.
  mustn't        CLOSES one.

FORM — like can, not like have to
  plain verb, and it never changes
     I must, she must, they must  (no -s)
  no do in questions or negatives
     Must I go?    You mustn't.

WHERE YOU MEET IT:
  You will READ must far more than you
  say it. Signs, contracts and notices
  use it; speech usually uses have to.
grammar.workedExample:
A safety notice says: you must not operate the lifting equipment without training.
1. Find the form: must not. That forbids.
2. What exactly is forbidden? Operating it without training — not operating it at all.
3. So if you have been trained, you may operate it. The prohibition is conditional.
Now the contrast. The same notice says you do not have to wear a helmet in this bay.
1. Find the form: do not have to. That is Unit 11, and it opens.
2. So a helmet is not required here. You may wear one if you want.
3. Check you did not read it as forbidden — nothing on that line forbids anything.
One notice, both forms, opposite meanings. Read the form first and the meaning follows.
grammar.mistake: Reading mustn't as merely optional, or reading do not have to as forbidden. These are the two halves of the same confusion and they fail in opposite directions. The other error is grammatical: adding do — do you must go, I do not must. Must behaves like can from Unit 3 and makes its own questions and negatives.
grammar.tip: Don't have to opens. Mustn't closes.
grammar.practice:
Write must, mustn't or don't have to.
1. You ____ wear safety shoes. It is a rule.
2. You ____ enter this area. It is forbidden.
3. You ____ wear a helmet in this bay. It is not required.
4. All staff ____ sign in.
5. You ____ use an extinguisher without training.
6. You ____ have experience. Anyone can apply.
grammar.answers:
1. must  2. mustn't  3. don't have to  4. must  5. mustn't  6. don't have to
Numbers 3 and 6 are the open doors — nothing is forbidden in either. Numbers 2 and 5 are the closed ones.
If you put mustn't in 3 or 6, read the second sentence of each again: not required and anyone can apply both say the opposite of forbidden.

grammar.title: Three ways to say allowed and not allowed
grammar.explanation: The same rule can be expressed three ways, and which one you meet tells you who is speaking and how direct they are being.
grammar.rule:
1  CAN / CANNOT — permission (Unit 3's can)
     You can park here.
     You can't park here.

2  NO + -ING — the sign form
     No smoking.       No parking.
     No entry.         No eating or drinking.
     Two words. No verb, no subject, no modal.

3  ALLOWED / NOT ALLOWED — the explanation
     Smoking is not allowed in here.
     You're not allowed to park there.

THREE REGISTERS, ONE RULE:
  No smoking.              the sign
  Smoking isn't allowed.   the explanation
  You mustn't smoke here.  the instruction

WATCH THE FORM AFTER EACH:
  no + verb-ING       no parking
  allowed + TO + verb  not allowed to park
  mustn't + PLAIN     mustn't park
grammar.workedExample:
You need to tell a colleague that smoking is against the rules here.
1. Which register fits? A colleague explaining a rule to another person uses allowed.
2. Build it: allowed takes to plus the plain verb — you're not allowed to smoke in here.
3. Compare the alternatives. The sign on the wall says no smoking, with -ing. An instruction from a supervisor would be you mustn't smoke here, with the plain verb.
Three forms, three verb shapes, and getting the shape wrong is the usual error: no smoke, not allowed smoking, mustn't to smoke are each wrong in a different way.
The rule to hold: no takes -ing, allowed takes to, mustn't takes the plain verb.
grammar.mistake: Mixing the verb forms between the three structures — no smoke instead of no smoking, or not allowed smoking instead of not allowed to smoke. Each structure takes a different shape and they do not swap. The other error is register: writing you mustn't smoke as a sign, where English writes no smoking, and saying no smoking to a colleague, where English says it isn't allowed.
grammar.tip: No takes -ing. Allowed takes to. Mustn't takes the plain verb.
grammar.practice:
Write the same rule three ways: as a sign, as an explanation, and as an instruction.
1. Smoking is against the rules here.
2. Parking is against the rules here.
3. Eating is against the rules in this room.
4. Going in is against the rules for most people.
grammar.answers:
1. No smoking. / Smoking isn't allowed in here. / You mustn't smoke here.
2. No parking. / You aren't allowed to park here. / You mustn't park here.
3. No eating. / Eating isn't allowed in this room. / You mustn't eat in here.
4. No entry. / You aren't allowed in without permission. / You mustn't go in.
Check the verb shape in each column. Signs have -ing, explanations have to plus a plain verb, instructions have a plain verb straight after mustn't.
Number 4 is the odd one, because the sign form uses a noun — entry — rather than an -ing verb. English signs use both, and entry, exit and access are the common nouns.

grammar.title: Reading a public sign
grammar.explanation: Signs delete words. Reading one means putting them back, and there are three questions that do it — plus one habit that prevents the commonest error.
grammar.rule:
SIGNS DELETE WORDS. PUT THEM BACK.
  Mind the step.
     -> You should mind the step.
  Danger: deep water.
     -> There is deep water. Stay away.
  Authorised personnel only.
     -> Only authorised personnel may enter.

THREE QUESTIONS
  1  WHO is it addressed to?
       staff only  vs  authorised personnel only
       (a group you're in / a permission given)
  2  INSTRUCTION or INFORMATION?
       Mind the step   -> tells you what to do
       Deep water      -> tells you a fact
  3  WHAT IF YOU IGNORE IT?
       a fine   -> a rule, enforced by somebody
       deep water -> a warning, enforced by physics

THE COMMONEST ERROR:
  the most important word is often the LAST
     No parking.                    absolute
     No parking between 8am and 6pm. not
     No parking except for loading.  not

  Read every sign to the END.
  Short signs are the riskiest.
grammar.workedExample:
You see a sign reading NO PARKING, and underneath, in smaller letters, except for loading.
1. Read to the end. Do not stop at the second word.
2. Reconstruct: parking is not allowed here, except when you are loading.
3. Question 1 — who is it for? Everybody, but the exception applies only to people loading.
4. Question 2 — instruction or information? Instruction.
5. Question 3 — what if you ignore it? Parking rules are usually enforced by a fine, so this is a rule rather than a warning.
Result: you may stop here to load, and you may not leave the vehicle there.
Had you stopped reading at NO PARKING, you would have driven away confident that you had understood a sign that said something else.
grammar.mistake: Stopping at the second word. This is the commonest error with English signage and it produces a confident misreading rather than an uncertain one, which is why it is dangerous. The other error is treating staff only and authorised personnel only as the same thing — being staff does not make you authorised, and the second sign is much narrower.
grammar.tip: Read to the end. The qualifier is always last.
grammar.practice:
Write the full sentence each sign stands for, then say who it addresses.
1. Mind the step.
2. No entry.
3. Authorised personnel only.
4. Danger: deep excavation.
5. No parking except for loading.
6. Keep the escape route clear at all times.
grammar.answers:
1. You should mind the step. — everybody
2. You may not enter here. — everybody
3. Only authorised personnel may enter this area. — a named few who have been given permission
4. There is a deep excavation here and you should stay away from it. — everybody
5. You may not park here, except when you are loading. — everybody, with an exception for loading
6. You must keep the escape route clear at all times. — everybody, but in practice the staff who work there
Numbers 1 and 4 are information leading to an instruction; 2, 3, 5 and 6 are instructions outright.
Number 3 is the narrowest sign in the list and looks like the mildest. Number 5 is the one that changes meaning entirely in its last three words.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Six rules
speaking.instructions:
Say six real rules from somewhere you know — work, a building, a form of transport.
Three with must and three with mustn't.
Record them.
Play back and check the verb after must is plain and never has -s. She must sign in, not she musts sign in.
speaking.tutor: Say six rules and ask the tutor which ones forbid something and which require it.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Opens or closes
speaking.instructions:
Say each pair aloud, five times.
You don't have to wear a uniform. / You mustn't wear a uniform.
You don't have to have experience. / You mustn't have experience.
You don't have to sign in. / You mustn't sign in.
After each pair, say aloud which one opens and which closes.
Record one full set.
The second sentence of each pair sounds strange, and it should — it is a real prohibition and most workplaces do not have one. That strangeness is what makes the difference memorable.
speaking.tutor: Say six sentences, some with don't have to and some with mustn't, and ask the tutor which ones forbid anything.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Three registers
speaking.instructions:
Take four rules. Say each one three ways.
No smoking. / Smoking isn't allowed in here. / You mustn't smoke here.
Do the same with parking, eating, and going into a restricted area.
Record all twelve.
Play back and check the verb shape in each: -ing after no, to after allowed, plain after mustn't. Getting the shape right is the whole grammar of this card.
speaking.tutor: Say a rule three ways and ask the tutor which version it would expect on a wall, from a colleague, and from a supervisor.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Explaining a rule to somebody
speaking.instructions:
Say both sides, then change the rule three times.
A: Can I park here?
B: I'm afraid not — you're not allowed to park there between eight and six.
A: Oh. Where can I park?
B: The car park at the back is fine. There's a sign but it's easy to miss.
A: So the back car park, any time?
B: Any time, yes.
Notice B explained rather than forbade, and gave the alternative without being asked.
Record one full version.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor whether you can do four different things and ask it to explain each rule and give an alternative.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Say what the sign means
speaking.instructions:
Say the full sentence each of these signs stands for, then say who it addresses.
Mind the step. / No entry. / Authorised personnel only. / Danger: deep excavation. / No parking except for loading. / Keep the escape route clear at all times.
Record all six, with the who for each.
The last three words of the fifth one change it completely. If your full sentence did not include the loading exception, read it again.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor six short signs and ask it to say the full sentence each one stands for.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the notice aloud and act on it
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the whole safety notice aloud, including the headings.
Then say aloud: you have been trained on lifting equipment but not on extinguishers — what may you do and what may you not do, and why.
Then say what the fire instructions do not tell you.
Then read the four signs aloud and say which one you would misread if you stopped at the second word.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor the notice and ask what it would want added before it worked there.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A safety notice for somewhere you know
writing.prompt:
Write a safety notice for a place you know — a workplace, a kitchen, a building, a vehicle.
Use three headings: YOU MUST, YOU MUST NOT, and YOU DO NOT HAVE TO.
At least three items under each of the first two, at least one under the third.
Add an IN CASE OF FIRE section with at least four instructions.
End with a review date.
Then check: is anything under YOU DO NOT HAVE TO actually forbidden? It should not be.
writing.model:
SAFETY NOTICE — KITCHEN

YOU MUST
· wash your hands before handling food
· report any broken equipment the same day
· keep the door to the yard closed

YOU MUST NOT
· use the slicer without training
· leave knives in the sink
· prop open the fire door

YOU DO NOT HAVE TO
· wear the hat in the storeroom
  (it is required in the kitchen itself)

IN CASE OF FIRE
Sound the alarm. Switch off the gas at the wall. Evacuate by the yard door. Assemble at the far end of the yard. Do not go back in for anything.

Reviewed 12 March. Next review March.
writing.length: A full notice with four sections
writing.criteria: Three items under YOU MUST and three under YOU MUST NOT; at least one under YOU DO NOT HAVE TO that genuinely forbids nothing; at least four fire instructions in the imperative; a review date; nothing miscategorised between the second and third headings
writing.support: Write the YOU MUST NOT list first, then read each item and ask whether it is really forbidden or merely not required. Anything that turns out to be merely not required moves to the third heading, and that sorting is the exercise.
writing.extension: Give it to somebody who does not know the place and ask them to name one thing they still would not know. That is the line you left out.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Eight signs, written out in full
writing.prompt:
Find or invent eight short public signs.
For each one, write three things: the sign exactly as it appears, the full sentence it stands for, and who it addresses.
At least two must have a qualifying phrase at the end that changes the meaning.
At least one must be information rather than an instruction.
At least one must be narrower than it looks.
writing.model:
1. NO PARKING except for loading — You may not park here, except when you are loading. — Everybody, with an exception.
2. AUTHORISED PERSONNEL ONLY — Only people who have been given permission may enter this area. — A named few. Narrower than it looks: being staff is not enough.
3. MIND THE STEP — You should be careful because there is a step here. — Everybody.
4. DANGER: DEEP EXCAVATION — There is a deep hole here and you should keep away from it. — Everybody. Information, not an instruction.
5. NO ENTRY between 18:00 and 08:00 — You may not come in during those hours. — Everybody, at certain times only.
6. FIRE DOOR KEEP SHUT — This door must be kept closed at all times. — Everybody who passes it.
7. STAFF ONLY — Only staff may go beyond this point. — A group you might belong to.
8. THIS DOOR IS ALARMED — Opening this door will set off an alarm. — Everybody. Information, and the instruction is implied.
writing.criteria: Eight signs; a full sentence for each with the deleted words restored; who it addresses named for each; at least two with a meaning-changing qualifier; at least one that is information rather than instruction; at least one identified as narrower than it looks
writing.support: Walk one corridor or one street and copy signs exactly, including the small print. Inventing them produces signs that are too clear — real ones are shorter and more ambiguous than anything you would write.
writing.extension: Rewrite the two most ambiguous ones so that nobody could misread them. Count how many extra words it took.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the notice and the signs
writing.prompt:
Use the safety notice and the four signs in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. What does you do not have to wear a helmet in this bay mean, and what does the bracket add?
2. You have been trained on lifting equipment but not on extinguishers. What may you do and not do?
3. Which sign would you misread if you stopped at the second word, and what would you have thought?
4. Sign 3 says authorised personnel only. If you work in the warehouse, may you go in?
5. Name one thing the fire instructions do not tell you, and write the line you would add.
writing.model:
1. It means a helmet is not required in this bay, so you may wear one if you want. The bracket adds that helmets are required in Bay 3, so the rule changes from bay to bay rather than applying across the building.
2. I may operate the lifting equipment, because the prohibition applies only without training and I have been trained. I must not use an extinguisher, because that prohibition applies to any extinguisher I have not been trained on.
3. Sign 2. Stopping at NO PARKING would give an absolute prohibition, when parking for loading is in fact permitted.
4. Not necessarily. Authorised personnel only names a permission that has to have been given, not a group you belong to. Working in the warehouse makes me staff; it does not make me authorised.
5. They do not say what to do if the staff car park cannot be reached. I would add: if the car park is not accessible, assemble on the far side of the loading yard and wait to be counted.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 treats the two prohibitions separately; answer 4 distinguishes staff from authorised; answer 5 supplies a usable line rather than only naming the gap
writing.support: Before answering, go through the notice and mark each line M for must, N for must not, or O for the open door. Only one line is O, and every question except 3 turns on which category a line is in.
writing.extension: Write the one further prohibition you think this notice is missing, and say what incident would have to happen for somebody to add it.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the ten mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. She musts wear safety shoes.
2. Do you must sign in?
3. You do not have to enter this area. (it is forbidden)
4. You mustn't wear a uniform. (uniforms are simply not required)
5. No smoke.
6. You are not allowed smoking in here.
7. You mustn't to park there.
8. The sign says no parking. (it says no parking except for loading)
9. I am staff, so I can go into the authorised personnel area.
10. You must to wear safety shoes.
writing.model:
1. She must wear safety shoes. (Pattern 1 — must never takes -s)
2. Must you sign in? (Pattern 1 — must makes its own questions, with no do)
3. You must not enter this area. (Pattern 1 — forbidden takes mustn't, not don't have to)
4. You do not have to wear a uniform. (Pattern 1 — not required takes don't have to, not mustn't)
5. No smoking. (Pattern 2 — no takes the -ing form)
6. You are not allowed to smoke in here. (Pattern 2 — allowed takes to plus a plain verb)
7. You mustn't park there. (Pattern 2 — mustn't takes the plain verb, with no to)
8. The sign says no parking except for loading. (Pattern 3 — read to the end; the qualifier changes the meaning)
9. Being staff does not make me authorised, so I may not go in. (Pattern 3 — staff only and authorised personnel only are different)
10. You must wear safety shoes. (Pattern 1 — must takes the plain verb, with no to)
writing.criteria: All ten corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 3 and 4 are corrected in opposite directions; numbers 5, 6 and 7 each take a different verb shape
writing.support: Numbers 5, 6 and 7 are the three structures with their verb shapes swapped. Write the three shapes at the top of your page first — no plus -ing, allowed plus to, mustn't plus plain — and then fix all three at once.
writing.extension: Numbers 3 and 4 are the same confusion failing in opposite directions. Write two more of each.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Must, mustn't, or don't have to
activities.instructions:
Write must, mustn't or don't have to.
1. You ____ wear safety shoes. It is a rule.
2. You ____ enter this area. It is forbidden.
3. You ____ wear a helmet in this bay. It is not required.
4. All staff ____ sign in.
5. You ____ use an extinguisher without training.
6. You ____ have experience. Anyone can apply.
7. You ____ report damaged equipment.
8. You ____ stack above the marked line.
9. You ____ give a reason. It is optional.
10. You ____ keep the escape route clear.
11. You ____ block the fire door.
12. You ____ bring your own equipment. We provide it.
activities.answers:
1. must  2. mustn't  3. don't have to  4. must  5. mustn't  6. don't have to  7. must  8. mustn't  9. don't have to  10. must  11. mustn't  12. don't have to
Four of each. The don't have to items — 3, 6, 9 and 12 — forbid nothing at all. Read each one again and say aloud what the person is now free to do.
If you put mustn't anywhere in that group, the sentence after it tells you why not: not required, anyone can apply, optional, we provide it.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Open or closed?
activities.instructions:
Write OPEN or CLOSED for each, then one line saying what the person may actually do.
1. You don't have to wear a uniform.
2. You mustn't wear loose clothing near the machines.
3. You don't have to have a qualification.
4. You mustn't operate this without training.
5. You don't have to work weekends.
6. You mustn't prop open the fire door.
7. You don't have to bring your own tools.
8. You mustn't park in the loading bay.
9. You don't have to attend the Friday meeting.
10. You mustn't use the lift in a fire.
activities.answers:
OPEN: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
CLOSED: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
What the person may do, for the OPEN ones:
1. Wear their own clothes — or a uniform if they prefer.
3. Apply without a qualification.
5. Work weekdays only, or take weekend shifts if they want them.
7. Use the tools provided, or bring their own if they prefer.
9. Skip the Friday meeting, or attend if it is useful.
Every one of those five is a freedom, not a restriction. If any of your lines used cannot or must not, that is the confusion this unit exists to fix — read the sentence again.
The five CLOSED ones are all genuine prohibitions, and four of the five are conditional on something: loose clothing near the machines, operating without training, using the lift in a fire.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Three ways
activities.instructions:
Write each rule three ways: as a sign, as an explanation with allowed, and as an instruction with mustn't.
1. Smoking is against the rules here.
2. Parking is against the rules here.
3. Eating is against the rules in this room.
4. Going in is against the rules for most people.
activities.answers:
1. No smoking. / Smoking isn't allowed in here. / You mustn't smoke here.
2. No parking. / You aren't allowed to park here. / You mustn't park here.
3. No eating. / Eating isn't allowed in this room. / You mustn't eat in here.
4. No entry. / You aren't allowed in without permission. / You mustn't go in.
Check the verb shape in each column, because the three structures do not swap: -ing after no, to plus a plain verb after allowed, and a plain verb straight after mustn't.
Number 4 uses a noun on the sign — entry rather than entering. English signs use both, and entry, exit and access are the common nouns.

activities.title: Practice 4 — What does the sign stand for?
activities.instructions:
Write the full sentence each sign stands for, then say who it addresses.
1. Mind the step.
2. No entry.
3. Authorised personnel only.
4. Danger: deep excavation.
5. No parking except for loading.
6. Keep the escape route clear at all times.
7. Staff only.
8. Fire door — keep shut.
9. This door is alarmed.
10. No entry between 18:00 and 08:00.
activities.answers:
1. You should mind the step. — everybody
2. You may not enter here. — everybody
3. Only authorised personnel may enter this area. — a named few who have been given permission
4. There is a deep excavation here and you should stay away from it. — everybody
5. You may not park here, except when you are loading. — everybody, with an exception
6. You must keep the escape route clear at all times. — everybody, in practice the staff working there
7. Only staff may go beyond this point. — a group you might belong to
8. This door must be kept closed at all times. — everybody who passes it
9. Opening this door will set off an alarm. — everybody; it is information, and the instruction is implied
10. You may not come in during those hours. — everybody, at certain times only
Compare 3 and 7. They look similar and 3 is much narrower: being staff does not make you authorised.
Compare 2 and 10. The same two words, and the last five words of 10 change it from absolute to conditional.
Numbers 4 and 9 are information rather than instruction. Both change your behaviour without telling you what to do.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read the signs where you are
activities.instructions:
This week, copy down six real signs exactly as they appear, including any small print.
For each one, write the full sentence it stands for and who it addresses.
Mark any sign whose meaning changes in its last few words.
Mark any sign you had walked past before without reading to the end.
activities.answers:
No key — they are your signs.
What most people find: at least one sign has a qualifier they had never noticed, and it is usually on a sign they pass every day. Familiar signs are the least carefully read, because you believe you already know what they say.
The second finding is that real signs are shorter and more ambiguous than invented ones. Several will be impossible to write out in full without guessing, and noticing which ones those are is useful — an ambiguous sign is worth asking about rather than interpreting.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Find your assembly point
activities.instructions:
Find the fire instructions for a building you use regularly — work, a college, a library, a block of flats.
Write down: where the nearest exit is, where the assembly point is, and what the notice tells you not to do.
Then write down one thing the notice does not tell you.
If you cannot find a notice at all, write that down instead — it is also an answer.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: they did not know where the assembly point was, and they use the building every week. That is extremely common and it is the actual point of the task — the language work is small and the information is worth having.
The second finding is a gap. Most fire notices are complete for the ordinary case and silent on the case where the ordinary route is blocked, which is the situation the notice exists for. Noticing that gap is the same skill as reading a sign to the end.

quizzes.q: You do not have to wear a uniform. What does this mean?
quizzes.why: Don't have to opens a door — wear one if you like. Mustn't is the form that closes one, and the two are opposite meanings.

quizzes.q: You must not wear a uniform. What does this mean?
quizzes.why: Mustn't forbids. This and the previous question are the pair the whole unit is built around, and they are one small word apart.

options: She must to wear safety shoes.
quizzes.why: Must takes the plain verb and never changes for person — no -s, no to. It behaves like can from Unit 3, not like have to from Unit 11.

quizzes.q: Which is the correct sign form?
quizzes.why: No takes the -ing form. It is two words standing for a whole prohibition, with no verb, subject or modal.

options: You are not allowed to smoke in here.
You are not allowed smoking in here.
You are not allowed smoke in here.
You are not allow to smoke in here.
quizzes.a: You are not allowed to smoke in here.
quizzes.why: Allowed takes to plus a plain verb. Each of the three structures takes a different shape and they do not swap.

quizzes.q: A sign says NO PARKING except for loading. What does it mean?
options: You may park here at any time
You may stop to load, but not park
quizzes.a: You may stop to load, but not park
quizzes.why: The qualifier is at the end and it changes the sign completely. Stopping at the second word produces a confident misreading.

quizzes.q: What does authorised personnel only stand for in full?
options: Only authorised personnel may enter this area
quizzes.a: Only authorised personnel may enter this area
quizzes.why: The sign has deleted a verb, a modal and an object. Reconstructing all three is the skill, and the reconstruction shows how narrow it is.

quizzes.q: You work in the warehouse. A door says AUTHORISED PERSONNEL ONLY. May you go in?
options: Yes, warehouse staff are always authorised
Not necessarily — being staff is not the same as being authorised
Yes, if you are wearing safety shoes
quizzes.a: Not necessarily — being staff is not the same as being authorised
quizzes.why: Staff only names a group you might belong to; authorised personnel only names a permission you have to have been given. The two signs look alike and one is much narrower.
Must makes its own questions and negatives with no do at all, exactly like can. Have to is the one that needs do.

quizzes.q: Reading 2 says the most important word on a sign is often the last. Why?
options: Signs are read from the bottom
The qualifying phrase comes at the end
The last word is always larger
It names who wrote the sign
quizzes.a: The qualifying phrase comes at the end
quizzes.why: No parking is absolute; no parking between 8am and 6pm is not. Short signs are the riskiest because you believe you have already understood them.

quizzes.q: The notice forbids operating lifting equipment without training. You have been trained. What follows?
options: You may operate it — the prohibition is conditional
You still may not operate it
You may operate it only with a supervisor
The notice does not apply to you at all
quizzes.a: You may operate it — the prohibition is conditional
quizzes.why: The prohibition attaches to operating it without training, not to operating it at all. Reading it as absolute gets the answer wrong.

quizzes.q: Which sign is information rather than an instruction?
quizzes.why: It states a fact and leaves the conclusion to you. The other three tell you what to do. Both kinds change your behaviour; only one tells you how.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it is built in two columns on purpose — sorting OPEN from CLOSED is the easy half, and writing what the person may actually do is the half that shows whether the meaning has landed. Practices 5 and 6 are field tasks with no key and both carry a what-most-people-find note.

teacherNotes.type: The six-unit gap is the design
teacherNotes.note: Unit 11 owns have to and don't have to; this unit owns must and mustn't. They are the two halves of one confusion and they are deliberately far apart, because learners who meet both in one lesson blur them permanently. Every negative in Unit 11 opened a door; this unit is the first place a prohibition form appears at all. Reading 1 states the separation and its reason explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

teacherNotes.type: Must is read more than it is said
teacherNotes.note: In speech, have to is far more common for obligation. Must dominates written rules — signs, contracts, safety notices, official instructions. The practical consequence is that mustn't needs to be recognised instantly and produced only occasionally, which is why the unit's reading load is heavier than its speaking load and why Speaking 2 drills the contrast rather than the production.

No plus -ing, allowed plus to, mustn't plus the plain verb. The errors are almost entirely shape-swapping, and Writing 4 numbers 5, 6 and 7 are that trio deliberately adjacent. The register point matters as much as the grammar: no smoking on a wall, it isn't allowed from a colleague, you mustn't from a supervisor. A learner who says no smoking to a colleague is grammatically correct and socially odd.

teacherNotes.type: Reading to the end is the highest-value habit
teacherNotes.note: The qualifier-at-the-end error produces a confident misreading rather than an uncertain one, which is what makes it dangerous, and it happens to first-language readers too. Sign 2 in Reading 3 is that error made available to catch. Practice 5 asks learners to find a real example, and most will find one on a sign they pass daily — familiar signs are the least carefully read.

teacherNotes.type: Why the notice has an open door on it
teacherNotes.note: The YOU DO NOT HAVE TO heading sits directly beneath six prohibitions, which is exactly where the Unit 11 confusion would surface if the separation had not worked. It also carries a bracket showing the rule changes by location, so the learner cannot generalise it across the building. Writing 1 asks learners to build the same three-heading structure and then audit their own second and third lists for miscategorisation.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Practice 5 and Practice 6 send learners to look at real signs and real fire notices in buildings they use: the name and location of those buildings must never be collected, shared or entered into the app. Practice 6 asks for the exit, the assembly point and one gap — not for where the learner works or lives — and that wording should stay. Practice 6 also has a genuine safety value beyond the language: a learner who finishes it knows their assembly point, and most did not before.

selfAssessment.statement: I can tell the difference between something that is not required and something that is forbidden.
I can say a rule three ways and choose the one that fits the situation.
I can read a short sign and say the full sentence it is standing in for.
I can read a safety notice and know exactly what I must and must not do.

assignment.title: A notice written, and a notice read
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, write the safety notice from Writing 1 for a place you know, with all four sections, then audit your own YOU DO NOT HAVE TO list aloud and record one sentence for each item confirming it forbids nothing. Second, write full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3 about the notice and signs in Reading 3, and add the eight signs from Writing 2 written out in full with who each one addresses. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written answers
